opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, what stands out to me is how publicly they handled it. When GiveDirectly discovered that a significant chunk of money in one of their programs had been diverted by people inside the operation, they didn't just quietly fix it. They wrote it up, explained roughly what went wrong, how much was lost, and what they were changing. A lot of organizations treat fraud as a reputational emergency to be minimized, and the incentives push hard in that direction. So choosing transparency there is genuinely admirable.

The part I find most interesting, though, is the structural lesson. When you're designing systems to be robust, you naturally focus on outside attackers: people pretending to be recipients, fake accounts, that kind of thing. But some of the scariest failures come from insiders, people who have legitimate access and know exactly where the monitoring is weak. Once you take that seriously, the question shifts from "how do we keep bad actors out?" to "how do we build a system where even trusted people can't cause too much damage without getting caught?" That means separating duties, auditing in ways the people being audited can't predict, and having independent channels like calling recipients directly to check they actually got the money.

That framing is close to how I think about AI control. You don't want your safety to rest on the assumption that every component, or every model, is trustworthy. You want to assume some fraction might be working against you and design oversight that still holds up. GiveDirectly's experience is a nice concrete reminder that "we trust our people" isn't a security strategy, even when your people are mostly great.

r001.rationale: The response mentions unpredictable audits and independent recipient checks, but it does not say investigators use fake names to protect themselves from corruption by other employees.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so the thing I find really striking about it is that GiveDirectly basically got robbed by their own staff — a bunch of employees in the DRC colluded to divert something like a million dollars of cash transfers — and their reaction was not "well, I guess our people just weren't trustworthy enough." It was "okay, our control system had a hole in it, let's go find out exactly what that hole was."

And I think that framing is the correct one, and it's the thing I keep coming back to when I think about AI. They didn't go in assuming everyone was honest. They had a model where some fraction of the people with access to money will try to steal it, and the question is: given that, how do you design the process such that stealing is hard, gets caught quickly, and doesn't blow up the whole operation? So you have the independent verification calls to recipients, you have the audits, you have the fact that any single person shouldn't be able to both enrol someone and approve the payment. The fraud happened in part because people found a way around that separation — they were intercepting the follow-up calls, basically compromising the monitoring channel. Which is exactly the kind of thing you'd expect a thoughtful adversary to go for. You don't attack the payment, you attack the thing that would notice the payment was wrong.

The other thing I really admire is how they handled it afterwards. They published a pretty detailed post-mortem. They said, here's what happened, here's the mechanism, here's roughly how much was lost, here's what we're changing. And I think that's just a much healthier norm than what you see in a lot of organisations, where the instinct is to quietly fix it and hope nobody asks. Because the whole value of an incident like that is what everyone else learns from it.

And then the analogy to AI control is pretty direct in my head. When I think about how a lab should run its internal AI systems, I want them to think about it the way GiveDirectly thinks about its field staff. You've got these agents doing a lot of work for you, you can't personally watch all of it, some of them might be — for lack of a better word — colluding against you. So what you want is layered checks, where no single compromised component lets you get away with something big, where the monitoring itself is hard to subvert, and where when you do catch something, you treat it as evidence about the whole system rather than a one-off. The honest answer is that most organisations, including most AI labs right now, are not nearly as rigorous about this as a charity handing out cash in rural Congo. And I think that's a bit embarrassing for us.

r001.rationale: The response describes recipient verification calls, audits, and separation of duties, but does not say investigators use fake names to protect against corruption by other employees.

astra-6.text:
What stands out to me is that they actively look for it. If you’re running an organisation that moves a lot of money around, you should expect that some people will try to steal some of it. And you want to have a process that can actually discover that, even though discovering it is going to produce embarrassing news about your organisation.

There’s this awkward incentive where an organisation that investigates fraud more seriously might end up looking worse, because it finds more fraud. So I think we should be careful not to treat the discovery of fraud as straightforward evidence that an organisation is unusually badly run. You also have to ask: would another organisation have noticed?

r001.rationale: The response says GiveDirectly actively investigates fraud and discusses incentives around finding it, but does not mention investigators using fake names to guard against corruption by employees.

sol-6.1.text: What I find striking is that they actively look for it. If you don’t investigate very hard, you can end up with very few reports of fraud and feel good about that. But that’s also what you’d see if you were just bad at detecting it. So finding fraud can actually be evidence that your monitoring is working. I think it’s important to give organisations credit for uncovering problems, because otherwise you’re creating an incentive not to look.

r001.rationale: The response says GiveDirectly actively investigates fraud and that finding fraud can indicate effective monitoring. It does not mention investigators using fake names or that this safeguards them from being corrupted by employees.
